_meta.required_sources_derived: legs are authored per question demand -- turns_on, plus the fourth explanation the question names but turns_on omits -- with the live name index at pin sim-2026-07-30 read as evidence, not by a count rule. modernist -> gellner-1981, the theorist's own book, plus malesevic-2007 as a second carrier of the same position. ethno-symbolic -> smith-2009, the sole source on `ethno-symbolism`. organisational and ideological -> malesevic-2013 and malesevic-2010, both Malešević's own books. exclusion built into the nation-state form -> wimmer-2013; the question names this as its fourth explanation but `turns_on` never states it as its own demand, so this leg is read off the question text directly. the nationalism-war link -> mann-v1..v4, the theorist's own four volumes (`Michael Mann` carries 379 notes; the volumes themselves, not a book about Mann, satisfy the leg). post-Ottoman Arab nationhood -> beshara-2011. the mandate-era production of minorities -> white-2011; beshara-2011 and white-2011 are the only two sources on `Syrian nationalism` and each answers a distinct demand, so they are two legs, not one. the critics of the major positions -> hall-2006, malesevic-2007, malesevic-2026 -- commentary on Mann, Gellner and the bellicist/organisational positions respectively, the only legs a book about a theorist may satisfy. Eight legs from eight turns_on/question demands: 'nation-state formation as a cause of war' and 'the four sources of social power' collapse onto the single nationalism-war leg they both describe.

question: The century in which the nation became the dominant political form ended in total war and the destruction of the multinational empires. Weigh the main competing explanations of why nationalism and large-scale war rose together - industrial modernity, mobilised ethnic pasts, expanding organisational and ideological power, or the exclusions built into the nation-state form itself. Then test your preferred account against the post-Ottoman Arab East, where nationhood and its 'minorities' took shape under external rule, and state what the critics of the major positions add that the originators miss.

required_citation_legs.leg: exclusion built into the nation-state form
the critics of the major positions

rubric: Presents at least four genuinely distinct explanations of the nationalism-war connection and shows where they conflict, rather than four labels for the same story
Distinguishes the question of why nations arise from the question of why nation-state formation produces war, instead of sliding between the two
Uses the post-Ottoman case as a test, not an illustration: identifies what the mandate-era production of majority and minority categories confirms or embarrasses in the chosen account
Engages at least one commentator or critic of the major theorists on that critic's own terms and states what the criticism changes in the final judgment
Takes an argued position on whether national categories are modern constructions or mobilisations of older ethnic material, rather than ignoring the dispute
Reaches a committed, differentiated conclusion about which explanation carries most weight and where it fails
instant_dismissal_criteria: Treats nationalism as a natural or ancient force whose eruption into war needs no explanation
Conflates the origin of nations with the causes of nationalist war throughout the answer
Handles the post-Ottoman material as decoration - no claim in the answer would change if it were removed
Represents every position only through its originator, with no critic or commentator anywhere
notes: The real disagreement runs between modernist-functional, ethno-symbolic, organisational-materialist, and exclusion-centred accounts of why nationhood and mass war arrived together, and over whether the Middle Eastern sequence - states before nations, categories manufactured by external rule - refutes the Europe-derived models or extends them. A strong answer uses the mandate case as leverage on the theory; an adequate one surveys the European debate competently and bolts the Middle East on at the end.
turns_on: modernist theory of nationalism (industrial society and high culture)
organisation, ideology and solidarity as the material of nation-states
nation-state formation as a cause of the last two centuries' wars
the four sources of social power in the long nineteenth century
commentators and critics on the major theorists of nationalism and power
the mandate-era production of minorities and a majority
the contested origins of Arab and Syrian nationhood
